questions.question: Describe the full structure of Economics Paper 1 — sections, question choices and mark values — and explain the smart strategy for choosing which questions to answer.
questions.expected_answer: Paper 1 covers Macroeconomics and Economic Pursuits for 150 marks. Section A is the compulsory Question 1, worth 30: eight multiple-choice items at two marks, eight matching items at one mark, and six give-the-term items at one mark, where abbreviations, acronyms and examples are not accepted. Section B offers three questions of 40 marks each — one per main topic and one combined — of which TWO must be answered; each is built from short items worth 4 (two one-mark naming items and one two-mark application item), two ten-mark data-response questions scaffolded from easy to difficult, one eight-mark middle-order paragraph and one eight-mark higher-order paragraph. Section C offers two 40-mark essays, one per main topic, of which ONE is answered, marked as introduction (max 2), main body (max 26), additional part (max 10) and conclusion (max 2). Strategy: survey before writing; in Section B choose by the friendliness of the data stimuli, since data response and paragraphs carry most of the marks; in Section C choose the essay whose body headings you can map instantly; and never answer extra questions, since only the required number is credited.

questions.question: Using the practice table — goods exports 1 200, net gold exports 100, services receipts 200, income receipts 150, merchandise imports 1 400, payments for services 250, income payments 200, current transfers minus 50 — calculate the trade balance and the balance on the current account in full marking style, and suggest two corrective measures for the result.
questions.expected_answer: Trade balance = goods exports + net gold exports − merchandise imports = 1 200 + 100 − 1 400 = −100 million, a trade deficit. Balance on current account: total receipts = 1 200 + 100 + 200 + 150 = 1 650; total payments = 1 400 + 250 + 200 = 1 850; 1 650 − 1 850 = −200; plus net current transfers of −50 gives −250 million — a deficit on the current account. Full marks require the setup line naming the items, the intermediate totals, and the final answer labelled with sign, units and its name, because a naked number forfeits method marks. Corrective measures, each developed: raise interest rates to attract foreign capital inflows into the financial account, which finances the deficit; promote exports through incentives and trade missions to raise receipts; allow the exchange rate to depreciate so that imports become dearer and exports cheaper abroad; or apply import measures within the limits of trade agreements. Any two, explained with their mechanism, earn the four-mark follow-up.

questions.question: Plan the forty-mark essay 'Discuss in detail how monetary and fiscal policy can be used to smooth out business cycles, and evaluate the effectiveness of these demand-side policies', naming what earns the marks in each structural part.
questions.expected_answer: Introduction (max 2): define business cycles as successive periods of expansion and contraction in economic activity around a long-term trend — no borrowing of the question's wording, no announcing the plan. Main body (max 26), with every fact LINKED to smoothing since unlinked facts earn one mark instead of two: monetary policy in the downswing — the Reserve Bank lowers the repo rate to cheapen credit and lift consumption and investment, buys securities in open market transactions to inject liquidity, applies moral suasion; reversed in the upswing to cool excess demand. Fiscal policy in the downswing — higher government spending and tax cuts inject demand through the multiplier; in the upswing spending restraint and progressive taxation withdraw it; automatic stabilisers (progressive tax and grants) smooth without new decisions. Verbal graph: aggregate demand shifts right under stimulus and left under restraint along aggregate supply. Additional part (max 10), the evaluation: policy lags can land stimulus in the wrong phase; the Phillips curve trade-off means less unemployment costs more inflation; the repo rate cannot fix supply shocks such as droughts or electricity shortages; debt-financed stimulus builds future interest burdens; judgement — demand-side smoothing works moderately and is best paired with supply-side reform. Conclusion (max 2): one fresh closing judgement, such as that success depends on matching the policy mix to the phase and cause of the cycle, without repeating the body.
